blocks.content: A securityContext configures security-related settings for a Pod or an individual container, expressing, in Kubernetes terms, the same principles covered in the Docker Security module.

A securityContext can be set at the Pod level, applying to every container within it, or at the individual container level, overriding the Pod-level setting for just that one container, giving you both broad defaults and fine-grained control.

blocks.alt: Broad, Pod-wide defaults, with fine-grained per-container overrides available

blocks.content:
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: myapp:1.0
      securityContext:
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false

code.content:
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: myapp:1.0
      securityContext:
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false

codes.yaml:
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: myapp:1.0
      securityContext:
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false

blocks.content: These fields express, at the Kubernetes level, exactly the same concept covered in the Docker Security module's USER Instruction topic, requiring a container to run as a specific, non-root user rather than the risky root default.

blocks.alt: The exact same non-root principle from the Docker Security module, expressed in Kubernetes

blocks.content: This mirrors the Docker Security module's Read-Only Filesystem topic directly, making a container's filesystem immutable at runtime, so a compromised process cannot persist any tampering.

blocks.alt: The same read-only filesystem protection, now configured through Kubernetes

blocks.content: Exactly as covered in the Least Privilege Principle topic in the Docker Security module, capabilities.drop lets you strip a container down to only the specific kernel privileges it genuinely needs, rather than the broad default set.

blocks.alt: The same least-privilege capability dropping, now expressed as a Kubernetes field

blocks.content: A sensible pattern sets sane, secure defaults at the Pod level, applying broadly, and reaches for a container-level override only when one specific container genuinely needs different behavior than the rest.

blocks.alt: Broad defaults at the Pod level, precise exceptions only where genuinely needed

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: securityContext configures security settings at the Pod or container level, and it is where every Docker Security module principle (non-root, read-only fs, dropped capabilities) actually gets expressed in Kubernetes.
Setting sane defaults at the Pod level, with targeted container-level overrides only where genuinely needed, is the practical, sensible approach.
